🧩 Step 1: Setup — Load Core Packages

```{r}
# Install if needed

library(tidyverse)

```

🧠 Step 2: Load and Inspect Dataset

We’ll start by loading one dataset (say the Mendeley depression dataset) and run a feasibility inspection.

```{r}
# Read dataset (change file path as needed)
df <- fread("Data/smmh.csv")

# Quick overview
glimpse(df)
summary(df)

# Check for missing values
colSums(is.na(df))

# Sample text
head(df$text, 3)

```

📊 Step 3: Basic Dataset Diagnostics

These checks will tell you if the dataset is large enough, balanced, and text-rich.

```{r}
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)

# Loop through all columns and summarize basic stats
for (col in names(df)) {
  cat("\n==========================\n")
  cat("Column:", col, "\n")
  cat("==========================\n")
  
  if (is.numeric(df[[col]])) {
    print(summary(df[[col]]))
  } else if (is.character(df[[col]])) {
    # Frequency distribution for categorical variables
    print(df %>% count(!!sym(col)) %>% arrange(desc(n)))
    
    # Text length if it's open-ended
    df$text_len <- str_count(df[[col]], "\\w+")
    print(summary(df$text_len))
  }
  
  # Missing values
  cat("Missing:", sum(is.na(df[[col]])), "\n")
}
```

```{r}
# Sample cleaning
df$text_clean <- df$`8. What is the average time you spend on social media every day?` %>%
  replace_contraction() %>%        # expand "can't" → "cannot"
  replace_emoji() %>%              # replace emojis with words
  replace_url() %>%                # remove URLs
  str_to_lower() %>%               # lowercase
  str_replace_all("[^a-z\\s]", "") # remove non-alphabetic chars

# Compare before vs after
head(df$`8. What is the average time you spend on social media every day?`[1:3])
head(df$text_clean[1:3])

# Select numeric columns (Likert scale questions)
numeric_cols <- df %>% select(where(is.numeric))

# Correlation matrix
corr_matrix <- cor(numeric_cols, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

# Visualize correlation heatmap
library(reshape2)
melted_corr <- melt(corr_matrix)

ggplot(melted_corr, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red", midpoint = 0) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between Mental Health Indicators",
       x = "", y = "") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

```

```{r}
check_feasibility <- function(data, text_col, label_col) {
  cat("Rows:", nrow(data), "\n")
  cat("Columns:", ncol(data), "\n\n")
  
  cat("Label distribution:\n")
  print(table(data[[label_col]]))
  
  data$text_len <- str_count(data[[text_col]], "\\w+")
  
  cat("\nText length summary:\n")
  print(summary(data$text_len))
  
  short_posts <- sum(data$text_len < 5)
  cat("\nShort posts (<5 words):", short_posts, "\n")
  
  cat("\nMissing values:\n")
  print(colSums(is.na(data)))
}

# Example use:
check_feasibility(df, "8. What is the average time you spend on social media every day?", "14. Do you find it difficult to concentrate on things?")

```

# Mendeley Data Analysis

```{r}
library(data.table)
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)

tweets <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Tweet_Contents.xlsx")
nodes  <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Nodes_Data.xlsx")
edges  <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Edges_Data.xlsx")

# Quick structure check
glimpse(tweets)
glimpse(nodes)
glimpse(edges)

```

### Step 2: Identify key columns

Typical column patterns:

-    In **Tweets Contents** → `user_id`, `tweet_id`, `text`, `timestamp`

-    In **Nodes Data** → `user_id`, `label`, `followers_count`, etc.

-    In **Edges Data** → `source`, `target`, `relation_type`

    You can inspect a few rows:

```{r}
head(tweets)
head(nodes)
head(edges)
```

You’ve just confirmed what this Mendeley dataset really is — a **three-part anonymized Twitter network**, and your understanding of it is already spot on.

Let’s go deeper together into what this structure means for **your project**, what’s **possible** with it, and how to **turn it into a usable, analysis-ready dataset** in R.

## 🧠 Step 1: What We’ve Learned

You have three files:

1.  **Tweets Contents** → single column “Tweet” (text only, no IDs)

2.   **Nodes Data** → user IDs + follower stats (but no label)

3.   **Edges Data** → connections between users (source → destination)

    So this is a **graph dataset**, not a labeled classification dataset. That means there are **no depression/mental health labels per user or tweet**.

But that’s okay — we can **still extract rich signals** from it.

## 🔍 Step 2: What This Means for Feasibility

Let’s check against your problem statement:

> 
>
> “How can social media posts be analyzed to identify mental health signals and trends?”

✅ Yes — even without labels, this dataset is **perfect for unsupervised or weakly supervised analysis**:

You can study **language trends** in tweets about mental health.

You can perform **topic modeling** and **sentiment analysis**.

You can explore **engagement network structures** (who talks most about mental health).

You can even infer **clusters** of users/topics representing different emotional tones.

So instead of predicting depression directly, you can **detect mental health discourse signals** — still fully aligned with your topic.

## ⚙️ Step 3: What You Can Actually Do With Each File

| File | How to Use It | Techniques You Can Apply |
|----|----|----|
| **Tweets Contents** | Core NLP data | Sentiment analysis, emotion lexicon scoring, topic modeling (LDA), clustering |
| **Nodes Data** | User influence features (followers, joined date) | Correlate influence vs sentiment |
| **Edges Data** | Connection structure | Compute engagement networks (centrality, clustering coefficients) |

> You’ll get *content-based mental health signal detection* from Tweets,\
> and *interaction-based insight* from Edges + Nodes.

## 🧰 Step 4: Let’s Start With the Tweets File

We’ll begin by understanding the **Tweets Contents** file since that’s your main NLP source.

Run this in R:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)

tweets <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Tweet_Contents.xlsx")

# Basic checks
nrow(tweets)
colnames(tweets)
head(tweets$Tweet, 3)

# Text length stats
tweets <- tweets %>% mutate(word_count = str_count(Tweet, "\\w+"))
summary(tweets$word_count)

# Visualize text length distribution
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(tweets, aes(word_count)) + 
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) + 
  labs(title = "Tweet Word Count Distribution")
```

## 🔗 Step 5: Exploring Node and Edge Data (Optional but Valuable)

### Check Node Data

```{r}
nodes <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Nodes_Data.xlsx")
summary(nodes)

```

You’ll likely find:

-   `User ID`

-   `Followers`

-   `Followed`

-   `Joined Twitter Date (UTC)`

We can later **correlate user influence** (follower count) with the tone of their tweets.\
For example: do highly-followed users tweet more positively about mental health?

```{r}
edges <- read_excel("Data/Mendeley/Edges_Data.xlsx")
summary(edges)
```

```{r}
library(syuzhet)

tweets$sentiment <- get_sentiment(tweets$Tweet, method = "syuzhet")
summary(tweets$sentiment)
```

Or using NRC for emotion detection:

```{r}
library(tidytext)
library(textdata)
# This command will trigger the interactive menu. Select 'Yes'.
lexicon_nrc()
# 1. Ensure the NRC lexicon is loaded and named 'nrc'
#    This step creates the object that contains the 'sentiment' column.
# 1. ALWAYS run this line successfully BEFORE the pipeline.
nrc <- get_sentiments("nrc") 

# 2. Run the pipeline, but stop before the count() function
joined_data <- tweets %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Tweet) %>%
  inner_join(nrc, by = "word", relationship = "many-to-many")

# 3. Inspect the resulting data structure
print(names(joined_data))
print(head(joined_data))
```

🧩 **Goal here:**\

See how big the dataset is and whether tweets are long enough to contain meaningful signals.\

If average word count \> 10 → perfect for sentiment/topic analysis.\

If average \< 5 → many tweets are too short, and we’ll clean out the tiny ones.

## 🧭 Step 7: Summary of Your Current Standing

| What You Have | What You Can Do |
|----|----|
| ✅ Tweets file (text only) | NLP pipeline for sentiment, emotion, topics |
| ✅ Nodes file (user metadata) | Influence analysis (follower counts, join date) |
| ✅ Edges file (network connections) | Community-level mental health discourse |

This dataset **alone** can be your entire project if you frame it as:

> 
>
> “Analyzing Mental Health Discourse and Emotional Trends in Social Media Using Graph and Text Mining Techniques.”

It’s large, research-grade, and exactly fits CSP 571’s requirement for a semester-long project.

# Summary Generation :

```{r}
# ----- dataset_summary.R -----
library(data.table)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(readxl)

# List your files and friendly short names here (edit paths)
files <- list(
  Mendeley_Tweets = "Data/Mendeley/Tweet_Contents.xlsx",
  Mendeley_Nodes  = "Data/Mendeley/Nodes_Data.xlsx",
  Mendeley_Edges  = "Data/Mendeley/Edges_Data.xlsx",
  Stress_Reddit   = "Data/dreaddit-test.csv",                   # replace path
  Bhavik          = "Data/bhavik_mental_health_dataset.csv",            # replace path
  SMMH            = "Data/smmh.csv",                            # you already had this
  Students        = "Data/Students Social Media Addiction.csv"   # replace path
)

out <- list()

for(name in names(files)) {
  path <- files[[name]]
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    message("File not found: ", path)
    out[[name]] <- tibble(dataset = name, file = path,
                          rows = NA_integer_, cols = NA_integer_,
                          sample_cols = NA_character_)
    next
  }
df <- tryCatch(
  fread(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, showProgress = FALSE),
  
  # If fread fails, try readxl::read_excel
  error = function(e1) {
    tryCatch(
      readxl::read_excel(path),
      
      # If read_excel also fails, finally try read.csv
      error = function(e2) {
        read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
      }
    )
  }
)
  # If df is data.frame but not data.table, coerce
  df <- as.data.frame(df)
  r <- nrow(df)
  c <- ncol(df)
  # sample first 12 column names for compactness
  cols_sample <- paste(head(names(df), 12), collapse = "; ")
  out[[name]] <- tibble(dataset = name, file = path,
                        rows = r, cols = c,
                        sample_cols = cols_sample)
  # also optionally save exact column names to a csv
  # write.csv(data.frame(column = names(df)), file = paste0("cols_", name, ".csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}

summary_table <- bind_rows(out)
# write.csv(summary_table, "datasets_summary_table.csv", row.names = FALSE)
print(summary_table)
# End of script

```
